title: The guns that guarded Antwerp

facts.text: Antwerp, liberated on 4 September 1944, was the supply port the Allied armies needed. Once the approaches were cleared of mines, it officially opened to Allied shipping on 28 November 1944.
Germany answered with V weapons. The first V-1 flying bomb was recorded on 11 October, and the heavy V-1 bombardment began on 21 October.

To fight the flying bombs with guns alone, the Allies created a special and secret command in October 1944, Antwerp X, directed by Brig. Gen. Clare H. Armstrong of the US 50th Antiaircraft Artillery Brigade.
To keep their positions secret, the gun crews were strictly forbidden to fire at German aircraft. Their only target was the V-1.

The most effective weapon was the US 90mm gun, aimed by the SCR-584 radar, which acquired and tracked an incoming V-1, coupled to the M9 director, which aimed the guns along its path. The proximity fuze, which burst a shell when it came close to its target, had already made this combination deadly against V-1s on the English coast. Antwerp's gunners used it too.

A Signal Corps cameraman filmed one battery near "Mansfield, Belgium" on 29 November 1944: a 90mm gun with an M9 director firing, quad .50 caliber machine guns, a radar antenna, and a gun director with many swastikas painted on it.
Field Marshal Montgomery asked Armstrong to knock down 50 percent of the bombs that came into the area. A 1945 headquarters release said Armstrong was not satisfied with 50 per cent kills.

The command grew to about 22,000 American, British and Polish troops, with 208 US 90mm guns at its height. The guns ran 22 hours a day, and for much of December to March nearly every 90mm barrel produced went to Antwerp.
Of 4,883 flying bombs detected, 2,759 were accurately aimed at Antwerp, and only 211 reached the target area. Antwerp X destroyed 2,183.
Against bombs aimed at the vital area the kill rate climbed from 52 percent in December to 85 percent in March. In one six day stretch in March the guns destroyed 89 of 91, or 97.8 percent.
The last V-1 attack came on 30 March 1945. Antwerp X lost 32 soldiers killed, and its guns fired 532,000 rounds of 90mm ammunition.

photoNote: Tier: green. A hooded American gunner stands beside an antiaircraft gun dug in behind snowy sandbags in Belgium, the muzzle aimed straight at the camera; a radar dish (apparently an SCR-584) shows at far left. Original caption: Looking down the muzzle of a "Buzz Bomb Buster" that was stopped by neither snow nor cold. US Army Air Forces photo, National Archives 342-FH-3A05160-58967AC (naId 204840996), use Unrestricted, public domain. Print received 8 May 1945, so winter 1944 to 1945, not 29 November itself. Cropped from the mounted print scan (3628 x 4582) to the picture area, saved 1800 x 1228. The second scan in the same record is the Antwerp X press release used in the facts. The caption does not name the gun; it looks like a 90mm, but call it an antiaircraft gun unless confirmed. Chosen for the face and the muzzle staring out of the frame. Runner up: two soldiers on the wreck of a V-1 in the snow, "One of the 2759 V-1 robot bombs destroyed by the guns of Antwerp X," 342-FH-3A05275-60085AC (naId 204841193).
photoCredit: An American "buzz bomb buster" antiaircraft gun in the snow, Belgium, winter 1944 to 1945. US Army Air Forces photo, National Archives 342-FH-3A05160-58967AC, public domain.

declassified.fact: The gunners' worst headache was their own side. Even after Antwerp X closed the sky over its gun belts, friendly planes kept straying in: in the two weeks from 26 November to 11 December 1944, 357 Allied aircraft entered the zone.

film.shot_notes: Same reel as No. 101 (one upload). 7 P.M. (this card): "AA battery knocks out buzz bombs, near Mansfield, Belgium, 29 Nov 1944": 01:55 to 02:12 a 90mm gun with its M9 director firing (open here); 02:12 to 02:36 the battery and field in mist; 02:36 to 03:05 quad .50 caliber machine guns firing and crew close ups; 03:08 to 03:48 soldiers at the gun director painted with rows of swastika kill marks (CU 03:38 to 03:46), a battery of 90mm guns; 03:48 to 04:08 the radar antenna in silhouette; 04:08 to 04:14 a slate card (avoid). No shot here appears in the noon clip (06:39 to 08:24).
film.date_note: Filmed 29 Nov 1944 per the shot card. The place "Mansfield, Belgium" is the shot card's spelling and is unidentified; caption as near Antwerp's defenses in Belgium only if the facts support it, otherwise "in Belgium".
